articles.title: S3-Compatible Object Storage Backups Explained in Python (30-Day US/EU Retention)
articles.description: Short answer: object storage fits per-tenant marketplace backups when buckets stay private, restores use expiring signed links, and retention can operate in whole days; choose a dedicated backup system when immutable history is a compliance requirement. The decisive number is restore throughput, not the idle size of the archive. A nightly database dump that is cheap to retain but painful to retrieve during an incident is a failed backup design. For a marketplace keeping 30 daily snapshots per tenant in US or EU storage, I would separate the flow into four boundaries: produce the dump, transfer it, retain it, and authorize a selected restore. Infrai is a reasonable option at the storage boundary when the same team also wants one key and one bill across its backend services, while keeping the integration on plain HTTP instead of adding another provider SDK. That recommendation has a hard edge. It applies to ordinary recoverable exports, not immutable records. How can a Python app test US/EU S3-compatible storage for private data backups? Start with the restore objective. Record the largest expected snapshot, the minimum acceptable restore rate, the region in which the restore worker runs, and the number of simultaneous tenant recoveries the system must tolerate. I'm not sure any vendor comparison can settle throughput from a feature sheet alone; a timed restore drill with representative encrypted data is what resolves it. Your mileage may vary across regions and network paths. Then price the complete path: stored bytes, write and list requests, and egress during routine drills and a real recovery. “Cheapest” without that request and egress model is marketing arithmetic. Don't put the archive in a public bucket to make recovery easier. Keep it private, mint a short-lived download link only after an operator or tenant passes authorization, and log the snapshot ID, tenant ID, requester, and expiry in the application database. The object key should carry the dimensions the storage API can actually filter. For example, tenant/acme/2026-08-15T020000Z/db.dump.zst lets a prefix listing find one tenant without depending on server-side metadata search. Keep a separate catalog row with checksum, logical snapshot ID, byte count, region, creation time, and restore status. That database row is also the right place to prevent two workers from selecting conflicting writes because this storage surface does not offer conditional If-Match writes. One detail matters more than it looks: a 30-day policy is day-granular. Lifecycle expiry has a one-day minimum, so this design cannot promise deletion at 30 days plus exactly zero hours. Compliance language and user-facing retention text should reflect the actual deletion window. Retention policy belongs to application governance Object storage can hold scheduled database dumps, compressed exports, and restore artifacts. It can also return an expiring signed URL so a restore worker downloads one chosen snapshot without receiving the platform API key. The returned URL is its own credential — never attach the Infrai Authorization header to that request. It does not decide whether the dump is transactionally consistent. It does not verify that the marketplace can rebuild listings, orders, and payouts from the file. Those jobs belong to the database export process and the restore runner. This separation is useful: the producer emits a checksummed artifact, storage preserves private bytes for the retention window, and the restore service validates the checksum before applying anything. Large files sharpen that boundary. A single request is acceptable for a genuinely small export, but multipart upload should be a selection requirement for large snapshots because parts can be transferred independently and failed parts can be retried without restarting the whole object. AWS documents the multipart sequence as initiate, upload parts, and complete. Infrai's storage capability includes multipart operations, but multipart fragments do not have an automatic cleanup rule, so the application should abort abandoned uploads as an explicit housekeeping task. No shortcuts. Provider comparison after the constraints These options solve different ownership problems. The table deliberately avoids volatile unit prices; collect current quotes for the intended region, object size, request volume, and restore drill frequency before committing. Option Integration boundary Large-file decision When I would choose it Main trade-off Infrai One REST surface covering S3, R2, OSS, and COS vendors Validate multipart throughput with a regional restore drill A small backend team already consolidating several services and wanting one key, one bill, and consistent HTTP conventions No object versioning or object lock; GCS and B2 are outside its vendor coverage Amazon S3 directly AWS account, credentials, billing, and SDK/API Multipart upload is documented directly by AWS The team wants a direct specialist relationship and its own provider-specific controls Another credential, integration, and invoice remain in the operating model Cloudflare R2 directly Cloudflare account and direct API/tooling Benchmark from the application region The team wants R2 specifically and prefers to own that provider boundary Switching providers later remains application work Alibaba Cloud OSS directly Alibaba Cloud account and direct API/tooling Benchmark from the selected US or EU path Existing Alibaba Cloud operations already own storage and access policy Provider-specific operations stay with the application team Backblaze B2 directly Backblaze account and direct integration Confirm the intended upload and restore path directly B2 is an explicit requirement It is not available through Infrai's current storage vendor coverage The catch is the durability control model. Infrai's object storage is not suitable when policy requires WORM retention, object lock, recoverable versions after an overwrite, cross-region automatic replication, or permanent public links. Stick with a dedicated backup platform or a direct specialist offering the required controls in those cases. Browser-direct upload is also a poor fit when the team must self-manage bucket CORS, and static-site or image-hosting workloads should go elsewhere because public/public-read ACL is unavailable. For ordinary private snapshots, the consolidation benefit is concrete rather than cosmetic. The storage handoff uses the same bearer key and billing relationship as other backend capabilities, and its discovery surface publishes request schemas and runnable examples. That reduces credential and SDK sprawl around the boundary; it does not replace restore testing or turn basic retention into immutable backup. A Python API example for signed backup links This Python example uploads one already-produced snapshot to a private bucket and requests a signed restore link. It uses only the object write and presign routes, sets an explicit method, supplies an idempotency key for the write, honors Retry-After on a 429, and surfaces other client errors. The single-request upload keeps the example readable; route large production archives through the documented multipart flow after measuring the part size and concurrency that meet the restore objective. Set INFRAI_API_KEY, BACKUP_BUCKET, BACKUP_FILE, and BACKUP_KEY in the environment. The bucket must already exist and remain private. import hashlib import os import time from pathlib import Path import requests API = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1" TOKEN = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"] BUCKET = os.environ["BACKUP_BUCKET"] BACKUP_FILE = Path(os.environ["BACKUP_FILE"]) OBJECT_KEY = os.environ["BACKUP_KEY"] def request_with_backoff(method, url, *, headers, data=None, attempts=5): for attempt in range(attempts): response = requests.request( method=method, url=url, headers=headers, data=data, timeout=120, ) if response.status_code != 429: if not response.ok: raise RuntimeError( f"request failed with {response.status_code}: {response.text}" return response retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After") delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt raise RuntimeError("rate limit persisted after 5 attempts") payload = BACKUP_FILE.read_bytes() digest = hashlib.sha256(payload).hexdigest() auth = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {TOKEN}"} request_with_backoff( "PUT", f"{API}/storage/object/put/{BUCKET}/{OBJECT_KEY}", headers={ **auth, "Content-Type": "application/octet-stream", "Idempotency-Key": f"backup-{digest}", }, data=payload, presign_response = request_with_backoff( "POST", f"{API}/storage/object/presign/{BUCKET}/{OBJECT_KEY}", headers=auth, print(presign_response.json()) The printed response should be passed to the authorized restore job, which extracts the returned signed URL according to the discovery schema. That restore download must use a fresh request without auth; otherwise the platform credential crosses a boundary where it doesn't belong. In production, stream files rather than loading them entirely into memory, and compare a stored SHA-256 digest before the restore begins. Rollout begins with a restore drill Begin with one noncritical tenant and one region. Upload a realistic snapshot, list it by the tenant prefix, generate a signed link, restore into an isolated environment, and measure total recovery time. Repeat with the largest planned object and concurrent restores before choosing upload-part concurrency or declaring an objective met. Next, enable lifecycle retention and a daily check for abandoned multipart uploads. Keep snapshot catalog deletion separate from object deletion so an audit can distinguish “expired by policy” from “missing unexpectedly.” Finally, alert on a backup that was not created, a checksum mismatch, or a restore drill that exceeds its time budget. Delivery systems taught backend teams this lesson years ago: an accepted handoff is not proof of arrival. If this boundary matches the system — private files, signed restores, day-level retention, and application-owned recovery checks — start with the Infrai storage backup guide. If immutability is the requirement, stop here and select the specialist controls first. References https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.object.presign https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/ https://www.alibabacloud.com/help/en/oss/ https://www.backblaze.com/docs/cloud-storage https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS

articles.title: A small detail about JSON.stringify() and undefined
articles.description: I noticed something interesting about JSON.stringify() when dealing with undefined values. Take this object: The output is: {"name":"Alex","active":true} The age property is completely missing. I originally expected it to be something like "age": null, but that's not how it works. When JSON.stringify() encounters an undefined value in an object, it skips that property. But arrays behave differently. Here, undefined becomes null instead of being removed. I guess that makes sense, since removing an array element would change the positions of everything after it. There's also a difference between explicitly setting a property to null and leaving it undefined. // {} // {"name":null} This is worth remembering when sending JSON data to an API. For example: fetch("/api/profile", { method: "PATCH", headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" }, body: JSON.stringify(updates) }); The request body won't contain bio at all. Depending on how the API handles partial updates, an omitted field might mean "leave it unchanged", while null could mean "clear this field". Not every API follows that convention, though. Anyway, JSON.stringify() is doing what it's supposed to do. It's just easy to forget that JavaScript objects and JSON don't handle undefined in the same way.

articles.title: Bounding Shutdown Retries By Attempt Count Strands The Transcript
articles.description: By Rokas Remeika. Published 24 October 2026. When a voice agent worker shuts down, the framework gives it a fixed time window before killing the process. If your transcript persistence logic retries based on a maximum attempt count, the combined HTTP timeouts can exceed the shutdown window. The process dies mid-write, losing data that only existed in memory. The fix is to budget retries by wall clock. Give the operation a total time budget, and size it so the budget plus one maximum-length HTTP timeout remains strictly inside the framework's shutdown window. Symptoms Transcripts and end-of-call records go missing for calls that ended normally. The write operation is attempted, but the logs stop mid-attempt with nothing after them. The missing records look like flakiness, happening randomly across healthy instances. The failure gets significantly worse whenever the downstream storage service is slow, which is exactly when the end-of-call record matters most for debugging. What is actually happening When a worker process finishes a call or receives a termination signal, the framework running it initiates a teardown phase. The framework gives your shutdown callback a fixed window to clean up and save state. After that window expires, the framework or the host operating system kills the process entirely. Most persistence paths use standard retry libraries or custom loops that bound retries by attempt count. A network write might be configured to retry three times, with a ten-second HTTP timeout per attempt. This works perfectly during normal operation because the process will live indefinitely to see the attempts conclude. During teardown, the process is living on a fixed timer. A persistence path that bounds its retries by attempt count has a worst case measured in attempts, not seconds. Three attempts at a ten-second HTTP timeout can block for thirty seconds. If your framework gives you a twenty-two second graceful shutdown window, you have an eight-second deficit. The downstream service experiences a latency spike. Your first write attempt takes ten seconds and times out. Your second attempt takes ten seconds and times out. You start the third attempt. Two seconds later, the framework's shutdown timer expires. The process receives a SIGKILL while the write is in flight. The memory containing the final transcript is wiped, and data that existed only in that process is gone forever. The bound on your retry logic is real, but it is denominated in the wrong unit. Attempt counts bound the number of failures, not the time. Shutdown windows bound the time, not the failures. How to confirm it Filter your logs for the worker process ID that handled the lost call, starting from the shutdown signal. Expect to see the persistence attempt begin, followed by a hard stop with no subsequent log lines indicating success or failure. Measure the timestamp gap between the shutdown signal and the final log line of the process. Expect this gap to match your framework's exact graceful shutdown timeout limit, proving the process was forcefully killed. Check the downstream storage service logs for the exact minute the call ended. Expect elevated latency or HTTP gateway timeouts that pushed the write duration past its normal baseline, triggering your retry loop. Compare the recorded wall-clock duration of the shutdown callback directly against the framework window in your call event logs. Expect the duration to reach the framework shutdown window limit without any subsequent log indicating completion. How it works The fix is to budget the teardown persistence by wall clock instead of attempt count. You give the whole operation a total time budget, give each attempt its own HTTP timeout, and size them so that the budget plus one maximum-duration in-flight attempt still lands safely inside the shutdown window. Here is the sizing I run in production. The framework provides a 22-second shutdown await window. I give the end-of-call record write an 8-second total wall-clock budget. I give the HTTP client a 10-second per-attempt timeout. If the storage backend is struggling, the loop checks the wall clock. As long as the elapsed time is under 8 seconds, it fires another HTTP request. The worst-case scenario is an attempt starting right before the 8-second budget expires. That final attempt is allowed to block for its full 10-second timeout. The total time elapsed before the HTTP client times out and returns control to the loop is just under 18 seconds. That 18-second worst case fits cleanly against the 22-second shutdown await the framework gives me. The process has time to observe the final failure, log it cleanly, and exit on its own terms before the operating system brings the hammer down. The three numbers in that example are not the transferable part. The inequality is the transferable part: (total_budget + per_attempt_timeout) < framework_shutdown_window. You must write that exact arithmetic in a comment next to the constants in your code. The constraint is completely invisible from any one constant on its own. The next person to review the code will see an 8-second budget, decide it is too tight for a slow backend, raise it, and unknowingly break the system. They will not know what they broke because the increased budget still looks smaller than the 22-second shutdown window on its own. They will only find out when transcripts start vanishing again. What I would check first Check if the session was ended by a function tool calling a teardown routine rather than a normal caller hangup. A tool tearing down the session immediately can cut off final audio and disrupt the lifecycle sequence; if this is the case, arming a pending closure fixes it, as detailed in /blog/voice-agent-end-call-tool-truncates-the-final-sentence-or-loses-the-callers-last/. Check the HTTP response codes returned by the downstream API just before the data loss. An HTTP 400 Bad Request indicates a malformed payload that failed instantly, ruling out timeout starvation. If the downstream storage service returned an HTTP gateway error, the request completed over the network rather than being terminated mid-flight. Check whether the worker process suffered an unexpected crash or host termination prior to the shutdown callback running. Check process supervisor logs to verify whether the process ran until the framework graceful shutdown timer expired. Instrumenting the teardown path Fixing the timeouts stops the data loss, but you need instrumentation to prove the fix holds over time. A teardown sequence is invisible to standard request tracing because the client has already disconnected. I record the shutdown callback wall-clock duration per call and emit it as a structured log event. This allows me to query the duration and compare it against the framework's window across the entire fleet. If the persistence operation starts creeping closer to the 18-second worst case, I can see the degradation before it starts dropping records. Additionally, give an incomplete transcript write its own named failure code on the call's end event. Do not let it land as a generic internal error. When a failure code specifically names the persistence timeout on the end event, you isolate a wall-clock write failure immediately instead of investigating it as a generic error. Generalizing the pattern This failure mode generalises to every teardown path that performs a network write. Whether you are flushing metrics, saving an LLM context window, or writing billing records, the dynamics are identical. Anything you write at teardown that exists nowhere else in the system needs a wall-clock budget derived directly from the window you were given. Common questions Why do my agent transcripts randomly go missing on call end? Your persistence logic is likely taking longer than the graceful shutdown window provided by the framework. When the retry loop exceeds this timer, the process is forcefully killed, and the in-memory transcript is destroyed before it can be saved. How long do I have in a shutdown hook before SIGKILL? It depends entirely on your framework or container orchestrator. You must check the specific graceful shutdown timeout configured in your environment. Should I use a background queue for transcript persistence? Offloading persistence to a separate queue still requires a network write before the worker process is killed. However, you still have to successfully write the payload to the queue during the shutdown window, so the wall-clock constraint applies to the queue publisher as well. Why does setting my HTTP retry count lower not fix the issue? A low attempt count still relies on the per-attempt HTTP timeout. If a single HTTP timeout can exceed the framework shutdown window, lowering the attempt count still leaves the write vulnerable to being killed mid-flight.
